Jobs Edwin takes on.

  • Roof replacement

    Everything comes off down to bare deck. Edwin will tell you if any boards have rotted, then the new layers go back on in the order shown in the drawing below.

  • Roof repairs

    A stain on a ceiling or a drip in the attic usually traces back to one place. Edwin looks for the source and repairs it there, often at the flashing.

    Get a quote

  • Storm and hail damage

    After a hard storm, a look from up on the roof shows the bruised shingles and bent metal that can't be seen from the yard.

    New gutters and downspouts hung with a steady fall to the outlet, or your current runs rehung and resealed.

What goes wrong at each part.

Here's a shingle roof cut open, with each part Edwin looks at when he checks yours. Water gets in at the edges and the joints first, so that's where the checking starts.

A shingle roof cut open, from the gutter up to the ridge. Not to scale. Pick a number on the drawing, or a part in the list, to see what goes wrong there.

  1. Gutter

    Carries roof water to the downspout. When a run sags or spills over, a hanger has usually let go or the run has lost its slope.

  2. Drip edge

    A bent metal strip along the roof edge. It drips water into the gutter so it can't curl back and rot the fascia. New drip edge usually goes on with a new roof.

  3. Ice and water barrier

    A sticky sheet along the eaves, where ice can back water up under the shingles in winter. It usually goes down fresh when a roof is replaced.

  4. Deck boards

    The boards everything else is nailed to. Soft spots underfoot mean water has been getting in, and Edwin will tell you if boards need swapping out before anything new goes on top.

  5. Underlayment

    A sheet over the deck and under the shingles. It's the backup when water gets past a shingle, so it's usually replaced along with them.

  6. Shingles

    The layer you see from the yard. Hail can bruise a shingle without knocking it loose, and that's hard to spot from the ground. If the hail was big enough to dent a car or a gutter, have Edwin go up and look.

  7. Flashing

    Bent metal where the roof meets a chimney or a wall. Plenty of leaks start here or at a few damaged shingles, and those spots can often be repaired without a new roof.

  8. Ridge vent

    A vent along the peak that lets hot, damp air out of the attic. It has to stay clear, and tight enough that wind can't drive rain in under it.

  9. Soffit and fascia

    The fascia is the board the gutter hangs on. The soffit closes in the underside of the overhang and lets air into the attic. Both get replaced once they go soft or work loose.

  10. Siding

    The wall below the roof line. Cracked or loose pieces let water get behind it, most often where the siding meets the roof.
